title: Poetics (trans. S. H. Butcher), Parts VI and XV
key_findings: Part VI: 'Character is that which reveals moral purpose, showing what kind of things a man chooses or avoids'; tragedy is an imitation 'not of men, but of an action and of life'; plot = arrangement of incidents.

Part XV: four aims for character - good, propriety (appropriate to type), true to life, consistent; even an inconsistent model must be 'consistently inconsistent'; speech and action should follow necessity or probability.
practical_applications: Define character by the choices the person makes under pressure, not by a list of adjectives.
Use 'consistently inconsistent' as the rule for erratic characters: the inconsistency itself must be patterned.
limitations: Ancient prescriptive poetics, not empirical; 'propriety' reflects ancient gender/class norms (e.g. manly courage unsuited to a woman) that must not be copied.
license: public domain (translation); MIT Internet Classics Archive

title: Aspects of the Novel, chapter IV 'People (continued)'
key_findings: Flat characters are 'constructed round a single idea or quality'; 'the really flat character can be expressed in one sentence' (Mrs Micawber).
Advantages of flat characters: easily recognised and easily remembered; best when comic; 'a serious or tragic flat character is apt to be a bore'.
'The test of a round character is whether it is capable of surprising in a convincing way. If it never surprises, it is flat. If it does not convince, it is a flat pretending to be round.'
practical_applications: Short-form series (20 s clips, carousels) can rely on flat supporting characters; leads need at least one convincing surprise per arc.
Use the 'surprise that convinces' test in script review.
limitations: Literary criticism from lectures, not empirical.
license: public domain (US) / Standard Ebooks CC0 markup

title: Stanislavsky Method (Stanislavsky's System) - EBSCO Research Starter
key_findings: Lists given circumstances, emotional memory, method of physical actions, subtext, 'if', objective ('I wish to...'), super-objective (core purpose of the whole play) and through line (direct path to the super-objective).
Dates: My Life in Art 1924, An Actor Prepares 1936, Building a Character 1949.
practical_applications: Write each character's objective per scene as 'I want to + verb' and a super-objective for the season.
Use 'given circumstances' as the bible section listing facts the actor/voice must respect.
limitations: Secondary reference summary; Stanislavski's original texts not read.

title: The Art of Dramatic Writing: Its Basis in the Creative Interpretation of Human Motives
key_findings: Revised 1946 edition of How to Write a Play (1942) (per Open Library / Wikipedia).

Secondary sources reproduce Egri's three-dimensional character chart: physiology (sex, age, appearance, defects, heredity), sociology (class, religion, place in community), psychology (moral standards, ambition, temperament).
practical_applications: Use the three dimensions as a backstory checklist so behaviour has causes.
limitations: Book not read this session; content known only from secondary summaries (blog, thesis chapter). Practitioner theory, not research.

title: Engaging Characters: Fiction, Emotion, and the Cinema
key_findings: Proposes the 'structure of sympathy' as an alternative to the vague term identification: recognition (building a character as an agent), alignment (access to the character's actions, knowledge and feelings via narration) and allegiance (moral evaluation, sympathetic or antipathetic).
practical_applications: Diagnose engagement problems by level: can viewers tell who is who (recognition)? whose knowledge do we share (alignment)? do we approve of them (allegiance)?
limitations: Book not read; described via secondary academic sources (Kent repository, 2024 philosophy paper, Screening Characters introduction). Critics argue the levels are gradations of empathy rather than steps.

title: Defining identification: A theoretical look at the identification of audiences with media characters
key_findings: Identification = experiencing the text 'from the inside' as if events happened to oneself, adopting the character's goals and perspective; distinct from spectatorship, liking, similarity, imitation and parasocial interaction.
practical_applications: Separate 'do they like her' from 'do they feel from inside her' when testing a character.
limitations: Theoretical article; reused from registry (full text read by storytelling module).

title: Understanding audience involvement: Conceptualizing and manipulating identification and transportation
key_findings: Valence of information about the hero changed identification but not transportation; timing of the hero's deeds changed transportation but not identification.
Transportation predicted enjoyment; identification did not add once transportation was controlled.
practical_applications: Make the lead's moral information clear to raise identification; control pacing/timing of reveals for transportation - different levers.
limitations: Abstract and secondary summary only (Poetics 38:402-418); single film, Israeli student sample.

title: Young adults' wishful identification with television characters: The role of perceived similarity and character attributes
key_findings: N = 208 young adults; wishful identification (wanting to be like the character) higher for same-gender characters and characters perceived as attitudinally similar.

Successful and admired characters attracted wishful identification; men: successful, intelligent, violent male characters; women: successful, intelligent, attractive, admired female characters; humour was the only attribute unrelated to wishful identification.
practical_applications: For aspirational characters give visible competence and success; humour builds liking but not 'I want to be like them'.
limitations: Self-report survey of favourite characters (correlational), US college sample.

title: Mass Communication and Para-Social Interaction: Observations on Intimacy at a Distance
key_findings: Coined para-social interaction/relationship: media personae address the audience as intimate friends, producing an illusion of face-to-face relationship (per secondary encyclopedia and journal summaries).
practical_applications: A recurring character who talks to camera / to the reader cultivates parasocial bonds over episodes.
limitations: Original not read (paywalled); content from secondary summaries; observational essay, not experiment.

title: Parasocial Interaction and Parasocial Relationship: Conceptual Clarification and a Critical Assessment of Measures
authors: Jayson L. Dibble; Tilo Hartmann; Sarah F. Rosaen
key_findings: PSI (in-viewing sense of mutual awareness) and PSR (lasting bond) are often conflated.
N = 383: a woman who bodily addressed the viewer vs did not; the EPSI scale captured PSI better; the older PSI-Scale may measure liking.
practical_applications: Direct bodily address (turning toward camera) raises the in-the-moment sense of being addressed - a lever even for faceless characters (body orientation).
limitations: Abstract only; brief video stimulus.

title: The Parasocial Contact Hypothesis
authors: Edward Schiappa; Peter B. Gregg; Dean E. Hewes
key_findings: Three studies (Six Feet Under, Queer Eye for the Straight Guy, Eddie Izzard): parasocial contact with minority characters/performers associated with lower prejudice; mechanisms generally supported.
practical_applications: Well-written minority characters can reduce prejudice - argument for respectful, non-token representation.
limitations: Abstract only; mostly correlational/pre-post with student samples; US context.

title: The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives
authors: Melanie C. Green; Timothy C. Brock
key_findings: Transportation = absorption (attention, imagery, feelings); more-transported readers held more story-consistent beliefs and evaluated protagonists more positively; fiction vs fact label made little difference.
practical_applications: Character-led stories change beliefs even when labelled fiction - health facts in stories must be correct.
limitations: Reused from registry.

title: The Extended Transportation-Imagery Model: A Meta-Analysis of the Antecedents and Consequences of Consumers' Narrative Transportation
authors: Tom van Laer; Ko de Ruyter; Luca M. Visconti; Martin Wetzels
key_findings: 132 effect sizes / 76 articles: identifiable character correlates with transportation (rho about .20), imaginable plot .29, verisimilitude .27.
practical_applications: An identifiable character is one of the few story-side levers of transportation - but small.
limitations: Correlational; reused from registry.

title: Expanding Disposition Theory: Reconsidering Character Liking, Moral Evaluations, and Enjoyment
key_findings: Re-examines how viewers form and maintain strong feelings toward characters (disposition theory of drama); uses schema theory for how bonds form quickly and attitude/perception theories for how viewers defend them for the sake of enjoyment.
practical_applications: Establish moral alignment fast in short formats because viewers use schemas to judge characters within seconds.
limitations: Theoretical; abstract only.

title: The Function of Fiction is the Abstraction and Simulation of Social Experience
key_findings: Argues fiction models the social world via abstraction, simplification and compression; immersive simulation may aid understanding of others and empathy.
practical_applications: Theoretical rationale for character-driven educational stories.
limitations: Theory paper; causal claims later tested with mixed results (see Panero2016, DodellFederTamir2018).

title: Empathy (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
key_findings: Distinguishes contagion, empathy, cognitive perspective taking, sympathy/empathic concern and personal distress; critics (Prinz, Bloom) note empathy is biased toward the near, similar, cute and in-group.
practical_applications: Cute/similar characters attract empathy more easily - and that bias is an ethical issue in who gets designed as cute.
limitations: Reused from registry.

title: Reading Literary Fiction Improves Theory of Mind
key_findings: Five experiments: reading literary fiction (vs nonfiction, popular fiction or nothing) briefly improved affective (and in exps 4-5 cognitive) theory-of-mind test performance.
practical_applications: Historical example of a viral fiction/character claim that later largely failed to replicate.
limitations: Abstract only; see Panero2016, Camerer2018, FORRT_KiddCastano.

title: Does reading a single passage of literary fiction really improve theory of mind? An attempt at replication
authors: Maria Eugenia Panero; Deena Skolnick Weisberg; Jessica Black; Thalia R. Goldstein; Jennifer L. Barnes; Hiram Brownell; Ellen Winner
key_findings: Three independent groups, N = 792, four conditions: no significant RMET advantage for literary fiction.

Author Recognition Test (lifetime fiction exposure) consistently predicted RMET across conditions; most plausible: people with strong ToM are drawn to fiction and/or lifetime reading slowly builds ToM; verbal ability may confound.
practical_applications: Do not claim a single story makes viewers more empathic.
limitations: RMET is a narrow ToM measure; correlational ART link cannot show direction.

title: Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015
authors: Colin F. Camerer; Anna Dreber; Felix Holzmeister; et al.
key_findings: 21 experiments replicated with ~5x samples: 13 (62%) significant in same direction; replication effects about 50% of originals; non-replicating effects averaged ~0.3% relative size.
Kidd & Castano (2013) was among the 21; the original authors published a Correspondence arguing a different experiment should have been replicated.
practical_applications: Treat single striking findings about fiction/characters as provisional.
limitations: The per-study outcome for Kidd & Castano is in figures/supplement, not stated in running text; recorded as failed stage-1 replication per FORRT_KiddCastano.

title: FLoRA replication atlas entry: Reading Literary Fiction Improves Theory of Mind
authors: FORRT (Framework for Open and Reproducible Research Training)
key_findings: Lists 6 replications of Kidd & Castano 2013: Dijkstra et al. 2015 failed, Panero et al. 2016 failed, Samur et al. 2017 failed, van Kuijk et al. 2018 successful (close replication of Exp 5), Kidd & Castano 2018 mixed, Camerer et al. 2018 failed (supplementary Table 4, unsuccessful stage 1).
practical_applications: Quick status check before citing a famous psychology finding.
limitations: Volunteer-curated database; individual replications not all read here.

title: Fiction reading has a small positive impact on social cognition: A meta-analysis
key_findings: 53 effect sizes from 14 studies: fiction reading vs nonfiction/no reading gave a small improvement in social-cognitive performance (g = .15-.16), robust to sensitivity analyses, no clear publication bias.
Authors call for stronger manipulations and tests of real-world transfer.
practical_applications: Honest claim: fiction may slightly and briefly help social cognition; nothing about lasting empathy.
limitations: Abstract only; few studies; short-term lab tasks.

title: An Introduction to the Five-Factor Model and Its Applications
authors: Robert R. McCrae; Oliver P. John
key_findings: Five-factor model: hierarchical organisation of traits in Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, Openness; supported by natural-language adjectives and questionnaires across observers and cultures.
practical_applications: Use the Big Five as a character's trait profile (high/low on each) instead of type labels.
limitations: Abstract only; FFM describes traits, not motives or arcs.

title: How Replicable Are Links Between Personality Traits and Consequential Life Outcomes? The Life Outcomes of Personality Replication Project
key_findings: 78 preregistered replications (median N = 1,504): 87% significant in expected direction; effects ~77% of original strength.
practical_applications: Big Five trait-outcome links are fairly trustworthy - plausible behaviour for a trait profile.
limitations: Abstract read this session (registry entry was search_summary).

title: Toward a structure- and process-integrated view of personality: Traits as density distributions of states
key_findings: Experience sampling over 2-3 weeks: within-person variability was high - a typical person routinely shows nearly all levels of all Big Five traits; individual averages of these distributions were almost perfectly stable; amount of variability is itself a stable difference.
practical_applications: A consistent character still varies scene to scene; consistency lives in the average and the pattern, not in identical behaviour every time.
limitations: Abstract only; student samples.

title: A cognitive-affective system theory of personality
key_findings: CAPS: people differ in stable if...then behavioural signatures ('if A then she X, but if B then she Y'); variability across situations is itself an expression of a stable personality system.
practical_applications: Write character bibles as if-then signatures - consistency with room for surprise.
limitations: Abstract only; theory.

title: Cautionary comments regarding the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator
key_findings: Insufficient evidence for MBTI tenets; dichotomous types weaken validity; reported 5-week retest type stability 39-76% depending on dichotomy.
practical_applications: Use MBTI labels only as audience-familiar shorthand, never as a psychological model of a character.
limitations: Reused from registry; search summary only.

title: The Enneagram: A systematic review of the literature and directions for future research
authors: Joshua N. Hook; Todd W. Hall; Don E. Davis; Daryl R. Van Tongeren; Mackenzie N. Conner
key_findings: 104 independent samples: mixed reliability and validity; factor analyses usually find fewer than nine factors; no clustering work derives the nine types; little support for wings and intertype movement; subscales relate to Big Five as theory expects; some studies report usefulness for personal/spiritual growth.
practical_applications: Enneagram 'core fear/desire' prompts can inspire writing but are not evidence about people.
limitations: Abstract only; Journal of Clinical Psychology 77(4), online 2020.

title: An Experimental Study of Apparent Behavior
key_findings: Observers perceived simple animated geometric shapes as characters with emotions, intentions and other social attributes (as summarised in Ratajska2020 abstract).
practical_applications: Motion and relative position alone create characters - basis for faceless and minimal designs.
limitations: Original not read; known via the 2020 replication abstract.

title: Attributing Social Meaning to Animated Shapes: A New Experimental Study of Apparent Behavior
authors: Adrianna M. Ratajska; Matt I. Brown; Christopher F. Chabris
key_findings: 32 new coloured animated-shape videos (13-23 s) with social plots; N = 66 wrote narratives; participants spontaneously attributed social meaning, similar to responses to the 1944 film; people varied in how many social attributions they made.
practical_applications: Even 13-23 s of shape motion is enough for viewers to read a social plot - relevant to 20 s clips with faceless characters.
limitations: Abstract only; small sample.

title: Does the Kuleshov Effect Really Exist? Revisiting a Classic Film Experiment on Facial Expressions and Emotional Contexts
authors: Daniel Barratt; Anna Cabak Redei; Ase Innes-Ker; Joost van de Weijer
key_findings: 36 participants, 24 sequences of neutral faces in six emotional contexts: category choices and valence/arousal ratings tended to follow the context - 'some sort of Kuleshov effect does in fact exist'; eye tracking showed no expected condition differences.
practical_applications: Context (what we just saw) colours how a blank/neutral face is read - a main lever for faceless characters.
limitations: Abstract only; hedged result; earlier replications conflicting.

title: How Context Influences Our Perception of Emotional Faces: A Behavioral Study on the Kuleshov Effect
authors: Marta Calbi; Katrin Heimann; Daniel Barratt; Francesca Siri; Maria A. Umilta; Vittorio Gallese
key_findings: N = 28 Italians; neutral faces before/after fear, happy or neutral scenes: fear context made faces more negative and arousing (valence -1.25 vs neutral context); happy context shifted only category choices, not ratings; model explained ~10% of variance.
Notes only three earlier replications; Prince & Hensley 1992 found no effect.
practical_applications: Negative/fearful context transfers to a neutral figure more reliably than happy context - faceless happiness needs body cues too.
limitations: Small single-nation sample; some text/table inconsistencies.

title: Body cues, not facial expressions, discriminate between intense positive and negative emotions
authors: Hillel Aviezer; Yaacov Trope; Alexander Todorov
key_findings: At peak intensity, positive vs negative situations were discriminated from isolated bodies but not faces; perceived face affect shifted with the body.
practical_applications: For faceless characters the body carries valence.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Humans Prefer Curved Visual Objects
key_findings: Sharp-angled contours led to more negative attitudes toward objects than curved contours; authors hypothesise sharp transitions convey threat.
practical_applications: Partial evidence base for the 'round = friendly, angular = threatening' shape-language convention.
limitations: Abstract only; objects, not characters.

title: Understanding Comics: The Invisible Art
key_findings: 'Amplification through simplification': the simpler the face, the more universal; a realistic face is seen as another person while a cartoon face invites the reader to project themselves (via secondary summaries).
practical_applications: Rationale (craft) for faceless Mint & Tao: blank faces invite projection.
limitations: Book not read; claims are theory/craft, partly contested (the abstraction scale mixes two kinds of simplification).

title: How to Write Character Arcs (helpingwritersbecomeauthors.com; book 'Creating Character Arcs', 2016)
key_findings: Change arc built on the Lie the character believes vs the Truth; Want = conscious goal ('the perceived cure for the symptoms of the Lie'), Need = the Truth; Ghost = past event explaining the Lie.
Arc types: positive change (Lie -> Truth), flat/testing arc (holds Truth, changes the world), negative change: disillusionment, fall, corruption.
practical_applications: Template for multi-episode arcs and single-carousel micro-arcs.
limitations: Craft framework, untested empirically.

title: 'Breaking Bad': Vince Gilligan On Meth And Morals (Fresh Air interview)
key_findings: Gilligan pitched the series as taking 'Mr. Chips' and turning him into 'Scarface'; Walter actively chooses crime; a finite run lets characters change (per outlets quoting him, incl. TV Guide).
practical_applications: Documented example of a planned negative arc.
limitations: Page timed out; content from search results quoting the interview; exact wording varies across retellings.

title: Hello Kitty (Wikipedia article)
key_findings: Sanrio spokespeople have said Hello Kitty has no drawn mouth so people can project their feelings onto her; other statements say she 'speaks from the heart' or that her mouth is hidden in fur; the 1987 animated series gave her a mouth.
practical_applications: Documented commercial use of a minimal face to invite projection.
limitations: Tier E; press quotes partly contradictory.

title: Sonic the Hedgehog movie delayed to redesign the title character (TechCrunch, 24 May 2019) + NBC News 2025 report
key_findings: First trailer 30 Apr 2019 drew heavy criticism of the realistic CGI design; director Jeff Fowler promised a redesign days later; release moved from Nov 2019 to 14 Feb 2020; reported redesign cost ~US$5 million (anonymous source; early rumour $35 m); redesigned film opened to ~$58 m.
practical_applications: Case: a stylised character pushed toward realism broke recognition and appeal; listening and redesigning recovered it.
limitations: News reports via search results; cost figure unofficial.

title: Hank Azaria on decision to stop voicing Apu (Rolling Stone 2020) - coverage of The Problem with Apu (2017)
key_findings: Hari Kondabolu's 2017 documentary The Problem with Apu criticised Apu as a caricature of South Asian Americans; Azaria announced he would no longer voice Apu ('it just didn't feel right') after educating himself on representation.
practical_applications: Case: a long-running stereotyped character voice becomes a liability decades later.
limitations: Press coverage via search results; exact announcement date not confirmed (reported as January 2020).

title: Gemini image generation got it wrong. We'll do better.
key_findings: 23 Feb 2024: tuning to show a range of people 'failed to account for cases that should clearly not show a range', and the model became 'way more cautious than we intended'; image generation of people paused.
practical_applications: Case: blanket diversity rules in AI character generation without context produce inaccurate output; casting must be decided per story.
limitations: Company blog (self-report).

title: Easily Accessible Text-to-Image Generation Amplifies Demographic Stereotypes at Large Scale
authors: Federico Bianchi; Pratyusha Kalluri; Esin Durmus; Faisal Ladhak; et al.
key_findings: Ordinary prompts naming traits, descriptors, occupations or objects produced stereotyped images; stereotypes persisted despite counter-stereotype requests and guardrails.
practical_applications: Never trust default AI 'casting'; specify age, body, skin, setting deliberately and review for stereotype.
limitations: Abstract read (arXiv); models tested in 2022.

title: Prisoner of love: sexual violence on Thai television
key_findings: Sexual violence is a prevalent plot device in Thai primetime lakhon; the hero raping the heroine within a 'fated' romance is common and framed as legitimate; lakhon help regulate gendered behaviour (abstract).
Per search snippet: besides phra-ek and nang-ek, the nang rai (female antagonist) is the only other necessary character, with no male equivalent.
practical_applications: Thai archetypes (phra-ek, nang-ek, nang rai) are culturally legible but carry harmful scripts - borrow the legibility, not the violence or misogyny.
limitations: Abstract + snippet; Critical Asian Studies 48(4).

title: Representations of the Ideal Male in Thai Television Dramas, from 2013 to 2022
key_findings: Content analysis of 12 romance dramas: ideal phra-ek shown through plot (virtues set up early, solves problems, ends in marriage), appearance (handsome, uniformed, professional) and inner traits (wise, brave, generous, gentlemanly, responsible, kind, humorous, helps with housework).
practical_applications: Checklist of what Thai audiences are trained to read as 'the good man' - use or subvert knowingly.
limitations: Abstract only; small descriptive sample.

title: Main Character's Type of the Romantic Comedy Television Dramas of Channel 7HD
key_findings: Five Channel 7HD romantic comedies (Jan 2019-Mar 2020): leads mostly round characters; male leads gentlemanly, family-loving, forthright, reasonable, brave, with added playful/cheeky traits; female leads assertive, forthright, clever, strong yet sensitive in love.
Example: a near-flat 'good' hero (Phacharamontra) gains dimension through stubborn rationalism and cluelessness about love.
practical_applications: Thai mainstream leads use a 'good core + one comic flaw' formula - a useful local baseline.
limitations: Journal of Music and Performing Arts, Khon Kaen University; year not captured; qualitative analysis.

title: Queer Negotiations: Triadic Critical Discourse Analysis of Gender and Power in Thai Media Representations
key_findings: Desk-based CDA of Thai LGBTQ+ series, digital content and fan discourse 2018-2025: increased visibility coincides with persistent tokenism, commodification and regulatory intervention; communities subvert and localise global scripts.
practical_applications: Visibility is not the same as respectful characterisation; avoid token or comic-relief-only queer characters.
limitations: Abstract and introduction read; qualitative CDA, not audience research.

title: Complex TV: The Poetics of Contemporary Television Storytelling - chapter 'Orienting Paratexts'
key_findings: Viewers use paratexts (wikis, character charts) to orient themselves among complex TV characters and timelines; 'forensic fandom'.
practical_applications: Series need internal character references (bible) and sometimes audience-facing ones (cast cards).
limitations: Reused from registry (abstract).

title: The effect of the shape of eyeglasses on judgements of personality
key_findings: 39 Japanese undergraduates: imagining round glasses -> warmer self-rating; square -> more competent and stubborn.
practical_applications: Glasses shape as a character-trait cue in eyewear content (weak evidence).
limitations: Reused from registry; tiny sample.
